schools.summary: Augustine reads the verse of Christ, the Lord Man, who unlike the man of earth went not away in the counsel of the ungodly, came in the way of sinners by being born yet stood not therein, and sat not in the seat of pestilence, which he takes for the pride of rule or for hurtful doctrine.

Gill renders 'O the blessednesses of the man' (plural) — doubly blessed, temporal and spiritual — noting the psalm opens like the Sermon on the Mount; Calvin sets it as the Psalter's preface, reading counsel/way/seat as wickedness hidden, then habitual, then obdurate, though he doubts the three nouns really mount.
Henry traces three mounting characters (ungodly, sinner, scornful) and the descent of walk/stand/sit, 'none reach the height of vice at once' — the good man shuns them as a plague-house.

Clarke fixes ashrey (plural) and haish (emphatic, 'that man'), and a double climax — reshaim, chattaim, letsim, matched by walk, stand, sit; Wesley agrees standing exceeds walking and sitting standing, the scornful worst of sinners.

Ellicott cautions that the apparent gradation 'was a necessity of the rhythm,' not an epitome of sin's history, though the three terms keep distinct senses (Aquila 'mockers,' Symmachus 'impostors'), and 'seat' may be 'assembly.'

debates.question: Is the double triad (walk/stand/sit; ungodly/sinner/scornful) a deliberate climax charting the progress of sin, or merely a feature of the poetic rhythm?

sides.position: a studied gradation — sin's downward progress from careless counsel to settled scorn
the apparent gradation was a necessity of the rhythm, not an epitome of the history of sin

outliers.note: Reads the whole verse Christologically, of Christ the 'Lord Man' contrasted with the man of earth (Adam), taking 'the seat of pestilence' for the pride of rule or for a spreading, cankerous doctrine.

themes: O the blessedness of the man

schools.summary: Gill weighs which 'law' — not the law of nature nor the law of Moses as a fiery law that works wrath, save as it lies in Christ's hands, but the Scriptures, particularly the five books of Moses, the Law and the Testimony.

Clarke reads 'delight' from chephtso (will, desire, affection) — a doer, not a forgetful hearer, feeding on the word as sincere milk, the work perpetual; Wesley: 'day and night' means diligently and constantly, not seldom and slightly.

Ellicott: the 'but' is an elliptical strong contrast ('nay but'); 'inclination' is a bending toward the law; and 'meditate' is literally to murmur — of a dove, a lamenting man, a growling lion, a muttered charm (cf. Joshua 1:8).

Henry defines meditation as discoursing with ourselves on the great things of the word with fixed thought till we feel their savour and power, day and night, interwoven with the business of every day and the repose of every night.

themes: his delight is in the law

schools.summary: Gill reads the vau as 'for then shall he be' and the tree as 'planted' — not self-grown but transplanted, broken off the wild olive and grafted into the good, planted in Christ and the church, Israel's removal into Canaan an emblem.

Clarke stresses the cultivated (not wild) tree and unfolds palgey mayim as eastern irrigation, the 'watering with the foot' (Deut. 11:10) — fruit in season, leaf unwithered, deeper-rooting prosperity; Wesley: the leaf that withers not means happiness ever green, not transitory.

Ellicott renders 'So is he,' sets the image in its eastern climate (Ps. 92:12; Jer. 17:7-8), canvasses which tree is meant (rejecting the fruitless oleander for the palm), and reads the obscure last clause 'all that he doeth he maketh to prosper.'

Spurgeon dwells on the security of the planting (kept from the final uprooting, Matt. 15:13) and the never-failing rivers of pardon, grace, promise, and communion, warning that the prospering is not to be judged by sight, for the tried believer may feel, like Jacob, that all is against him.

outliers.note: Canvasses which tree the poet had in mind, rejecting Dean Stanley's oleander for its want of fruit and settling on the palm as best fitting every condition.

themes: the tree planted by the waters

schools.summary: Gill makes the ungodly the reverse at every point; if they are like trees at all, they are dry trees without sap, wild olives on a parched heath, fit only for the fire.

Henry hears the Septuagint's 'Not so the ungodly' and reads the chaff as the very lightest, the dust the owner drives off, of no worth and blown by every wind, the fan already in Christ's hand (Matt. 3:12); Spurgeon marks the 'ungodly' as the beginners in evil, the least offensive of sinners, yet chaff — worthless and easily carried away.

Clarke notes the Vulgate/Septuagint double negation and added clause and describes the eastern winnowing (grain falls straight, chaff is blown off); Wesley reads the chaff as the restless and unquiet, whose felicity has no firm foundation.
Ellicott confirms 'Not so the ungodly' and the winnowing of the wicked from the true Israel by the fan of God's judgment, an image so frequent as almost to be a poetical commonplace.

Gill takes it of both a temporal and the final judgment (Targum, Kimchi): the wicked are arraigned but shall not stand with the righteous nor with any confidence, and are condemned to everlasting punishment.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the 'therefore' in the chaff — inner worthlessness means they cannot stand in the mishpat, the judgment of just recompense; Ellicott marks the contrast with v.1 and reads 'shall not stand' as 'shall not rise / hold up his head,' shrinking away like the man without a wedding garment (Matt. 22:12).

Clarke reports the versional 'shall not rise again' and the annihilation opinion built on it, which he dismisses, taking the plain sense that the wicked will be condemned with nothing to plead; Wesley: not to stand is not to endure the trial, in the general judgment of the world.

Spurgeon presses the second line — earthly congregations are mixed (tares among wheat, one devil in every church), but no unrenewed soul enters the congregation of the righteous above, a sinner being as out of his element there as a fish upon a tree.

debates.question: Does 'shall not stand in the judgment' mean the wicked fail to be acquitted or hold up their head in a judgment they must face, or does the versional 'shall not rise again' bear on the resurrection itself?

sides.position: judicial — they shall not be acquitted or endure the trial that all alike must face
the Septuagint/Vulgate 'shall not rise again' was pressed by some into a denial of the wicked's resurrection (annihilation)
holders: some Jews and Christians (as reported and rejected by Clarke)

outliers.note: Reports the opinion of some Jews and Christians that the impious are never raised but annihilated, and dismisses it as 'unworthy of refutation.'

themes: shall not stand in the judgment

schools.summary: Gill insists 'knoweth' is more than omniscience (God knows the wicked's way too) — it is to approve, love, and delight in the righteous man's way of faith and holiness, his walk in Christ and his accepted sacrifices of praise.

Clarke reads 'knoweth' as approveth (Coverdale's 'aloweth') and tsaddikim from a root 'to give even weight,' the opposite of the reshaim who withhold right — men kept under God's providence; Wesley: God approves, loves, delights, and recompenses, while the wicked's designs come to nothing.

Ellicott glosses 'knoweth' as recognising with discriminative discernment (Ps. 31:7; John 10:14), and the perishing 'way' by the parallel that the desire of the wicked shall perish (Ps. 112:10), likened to a stream that dries up and vanishes (Job 6:18).

Spurgeon renders the Hebrew continuously, 'the LORD is knowing the way,' watching it through mist and darkness ('when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold,' Job 23:10), while the wicked but ploughs the sea, and the place that knew him shall know him no more.

themes: to know as to approve and love
the way of the ungodly shall perish
